extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors preparing and submitting manuscripts to academic journals (including early career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors on how the journal peer review process works, what reviewers and editors look for, how to respond to reports, and options after rejection. Includes descriptions of peer review models and publisher-specific practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers judge validity, significance and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to judge the validity, significance, and originality of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core remit of peer reviewers: to assess whether the research is new, important, and methodologically sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review evaluates quality and suitability for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of peer review is to evaluate the paper’s quality and suitability for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review acts both as quality control for journals and as constructive feedback to improve manuscripts prior to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate, trustworthy journal (Think. Check. Submit.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you submit your work to a journal you can trust by using resources such as the Think. Check. Submit. checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid journals that do not provide thorough peer review or editor feedback; submitting to such journals may mean you won't benefit from helpful peer feedback and may harm perception of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review integrity statement (editor screening, anonymous refereeing, revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should undergo rigorous peer review based on initial editor screening, anonymous refereeing by independent expert referees, and consequent revision by article authors when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the publisher's standard for what constitutes an appropriately peer-reviewed research article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-anonymous (single-blind) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers know who the author is, but the authors do not know the identities of the reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in science and medicine; check pros and cons for your field and journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-anonymous (double-blind) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither reviewers nor authors know each others’ identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in humanities and some social sciences; if submitting under this model, make sure you know how to make your article anonymous (remove identifying information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: A model where reviewers may know the authors and reviewer identities may be revealed at some point; there is no single agreed definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect variation in how openness is implemented; read the journal’s policy for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may be published quickly after basic checks and then invited reviewers or readers add comments or reviews after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your paper may still go through traditional review first, or feedback may be entirely post-publication; consider implications for versioning and responding to critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered Reports (two-stage review with in-principle acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is split into two parts: review of study design before data collection, and review of completed work after following pre-registered methods; passing the first stage can lead to an in-principle acceptance (IPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPA indicates the article will be published if the study is completed according to the pre-registered methods and an evidence-based interpretation of results is submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000Research open model: pre-publication checks then transparent post-publication review
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitted articles are published rapidly after pre-publication checks for originality, readability, author eligibility, and policy/ethical compliance; then expert reviewers are invited to review openly with reports and reviewer names published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest at least five potential unbiased reviewers; authors can respond publicly and publish revised versions; the article remains published regardless of reviewer reports; indexing occurs for articles that pass peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor initial (desk) assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors check if the manuscript is broadly suitable for the journal by asking: Is this the right journal? Does it fit the aims & scope? Has the author followed the instructions for authors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor will also check basic requirements such as word count, language clarity, format, presence of abstract, author affiliations, figures, and research-funder information. Failure can result in a desk reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum reviewer number and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimum of two independent reviewers is normally required for every research article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal’s aims and scope will outline specific peer review policies and any deviations from this norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assessment checklist (originality, methods, scholarship, presentation, conclusions, fit, standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers typically check that: your work is original; the study design and methodology are appropriate and described so others could replicate it; you’ve engaged with relevant current scholarship; results are appropriately and clearly presented; conclusions are reliable, significant, and supported by the research; the paper fits the journal scope; the work is of a high enough standard to be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This set of checks constitutes the substantive quality criteria reviewers apply across disciplines (subject to variation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data availability may be requested by reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have not already shared your research data publicly, peer reviewers may request to see your datasets to support validation of the results in your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to share data or explain why data cannot be shared (e.g., confidentiality, legal/ethical constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to reviewer comments: address all comments and document changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should address all reviewer and editor comments in revisions and may submit a two-column grid listing each reviewer comment with the corresponding alteration made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A point-by-point response helps order revisions and demonstrates to editors and reviewers that feedback has been considered. If something is unclear, contact the editor for advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disagree with reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If you disagree with a review comment, include an explanation of why you haven’t made that change with your resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend your position assertively and persuasively rather than defensively or aggressively; the editor will assess and include your explanation when sending the amended article back to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision outcomes and subsequent rounds
rubrics_metrics.description: After resubmission the editor will review revisions and may send the manuscript for a second round of peer review to assess the authors’ responses; further revisions, acceptance, or rejection may follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If revisions are judged inadequate, the paper may be rejected; if adequate, it proceeds to the next stage (production).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formally withdraw if you will not revise
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not intend to make the revisions suggested by the journal and resubmit, you must formally withdraw your paper from consideration before submitting elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids duplicate submissions and preserves integrity of the submission process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons manuscripts are rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical causes for rejection include: wrong journal (doesn't fit aims & scope); manuscript is not a true journal article (too journalistic or clearly a thesis chapter); manuscript is too long or too short; poor regard for journal conventions or academic writing; poor style, grammar, punctuation or English; the manuscript does not make any new contribution; research is not properly contextualized; poor theoretical framework; poor presentation; libelous or unethical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully consider reviewer/editor feedback and the journal’s aims & scope before choosing where to resubmit; address the specific issues raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer/cascade submission option
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paper is rejected for fit, publishers may offer transfer/cascade services suggesting one or more alternative journals within the same publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transferring can save time because you may not need to re-enter submission details; you should still make any necessary revisions and check the target journal’s requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI in the peer review process and reviewer restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-based tools can help editors find and match reviewers, but reviewers are specifically instructed not to upload unpublished manuscripts or associated files into generative AI tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher reviewer guidelines prohibit using generative AI on unpublished manuscripts to protect confidentiality and research integrity; tools can also flag competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time factors affecting peer review duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays commonly occur while editors identify appropriate reviewers and wait for reviewers to find time alongside other responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track progress via the submission system or contact the editor for updates; when choosing a journal, review published submission/acceptance dates for recent articles to estimate timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becoming and being an effective peer reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: To be an effective reviewer, learn how to become a peer reviewer, how to write review reports step-by-step, follow ethical guidelines for peer reviewers, and engage with reviewer recognition schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources such as publisher reviewer guidelines and COPE ethical guidance provide standards for conduct; reviewing improves your own writing and contributes to the research community.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000Research reviewer selection and openness requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For F1000Research authors are asked to suggest at least five potential reviewers who are experts and able to provide unbiased reports; peer review reports, reviewer names and affiliations are published alongside the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect transparent, signed reviews and public author responses; reviewers must be unbiased and comply with F1000Research policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000Research indexing condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles that pass peer review on F1000Research are indexed in Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar and other bibliographic databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial publication does not guarantee indexing; successful open peer review is needed for indexing.
